newsitem.title: UK: Safer headache tablet might be possible - study.
newsitem.headline: Safer headache tablet might be possible - study.

text.p: U.S. researchers said on Wednesday that a popular generation of painkillers including ibuprofen, preferred to aspirin in many cases, could be made safer now that they have found out exactly how the drugs work.
Ravi Kurumbail and colleagues at G.D. Searle & Co, the pharmaceutical unit of Monsanto Co, found the precise structure of one of the proteins targeted by the drugs.

An experimental drug being tested by Searle that is narrowly directed at this one specific protein has the same benefits of other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDS) but has fewer side-effects, Kurumbail said.
"If you take this drug, give it to animals and watch how they do, they do not get ulcers. That's one of the common side-effects of the NSAIDS," he said in a telephone interview.

NSAIDS such as ibuprofen and naproxen are popular drugs used for arthritis, headaches and general aches and pains. The group, which includes aspirin, can irritate the stomach lining, causing bleeding and ulcers which can sometimes be fatal.
They work by reducing production of chemicals known as prostaglandins. Prostaglandins help cause inflammation -- which can be a source of pain.
Another painkiller, acetaminophen, can reduce pain without hurting the stomach but has no effect on inflammation.
The specific target of NSAIDS is a protein known as COX, which stimulates prostaglandin production. It comes in two different forms known as COX-1 and COX-2.
COX-1 has been well mapped out but Kurumbail and colleagues, writing in the science journal Nature, said they were the first scientists to use x-ray crystallography to look at COX-2.
NSAIDS go after both COX-1 and COX-2, but Kurumbail said the proteins play slightly different roles in stimulating prostaglandins -- roles that turn out to be vital.
"COX-1 is present in most of the tissues -- the stomach, the kidneys," Kurumbail said.
"It produces prostaglandins normally. You need those prostaglandins for normal functioning of the body."

COX-2 seems to be only produced in response to certain inflammations, which would make it the more logical target of anti-inflammatory drugs. "If you can inhibit (only) COX-2 you can avoid all the side-effects that accompany COX-1," he added.
Searle's celecoxib drug, now in phase three trials, targets COX-2 alone and Kurumbail said initial results were heartening.
"We think it think can replace NSAIDS," he said. "This is a very exciting area."

Kurumbail cited some studies that indicate people who take NSAIDS regularly have a lower incidence of bowel cancer. Some indicate that COX-2 may be involved. If so, Searle's celecoxib might work more efficiently against the cancer.
"Every company is looking at that aspect," he said. "With one pill you could take care of arthritis and cancer and that would be a dream come true."
